sounds.name: Your First Patch
sounds.ref: The basic Moog voice, cable by cable
sounds.blurb: One oscillator, the ladder filter and an amplifier, patched up one cable at a time until the keyboard plays notes.
sounds.how: A modular makes no sound until it is patched. This builds the standard voice: an oscillator into the 904A filter, the filter into a 902 amplifier, and the amplifier to the output. Then the CM1A gives the keyboard’s pitch to the 921A, which tunes the 921B, and its trigger fires two 911 envelopes: one opens the amplifier for each note, the other sweeps the filter.

steps.title: An oscillator through the filter to the output
steps.why:
The 921B’s sawtooth goes into the 904A filter, the filter into a 902 amplifier, and the amplifier to the output.
- Cables: 921B (1) SAWTOOTH to 904A SIG IN, 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +, 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 4: the filter wide open.
- 902 (1) FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 6: the amplifier fully open.
- Listen for: a steady buzz at middle C. The keys do nothing yet.

steps.title: The keyboard sets the pitch
steps.why:
The CM1A turns each key into a voltage. It goes to the 921A Oscillator Driver, and the driver’s output to the 921B’s link input.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A FREQUENCY IN 1, 921A FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ.
- Listen for: the buzz now changes pitch with the keys, but it never stops.

steps.title: An envelope makes notes
steps.why:
The amplifier is shut, and a 911 envelope opens it for each key. The CM1A’s TRIG goes through a multiple so it can fire both envelopes later.
- 902 (1) FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0: shut.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG (upper) to CP35 MULTIPLE A, MULTIPLE A 1 to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN, 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- 911 (1): T1 2, T2 6, E SUS 7, T3 5.
- CM1A TRIG MODE stays on S-TRIG, the kind of trigger the 911 needs.
- Listen for: separate notes that start quickly and fade after you let go.

steps.title: A second envelope sweeps the filter
steps.why:
The filter is closed down, and the second 911 opens it at the start of each note.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −2, REGENERATION 4.
- Cables: MULTIPLE A 2 to 911 (2) S-TRIG IN, 911 (2) OUT to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1.
- 911 (2): T1 2, T2 5.5, E SUS 3, T3 5.
- Listen for: each note opens bright and settles darker: the classic Moog “wow”.

context.m904a.fixed_cv: In this sound: where the filter sits between notes. The envelope adds to it, so higher makes every note brighter.
context.m904a.regeneration: In this sound: a little resonance at the cutoff, which gives the sweep its squelch.
context.m911_1.t3: In this sound: how long each note rings after you let go.
context.m911_2.t2: In this sound: how fast the brightness falls away after the start of each note.
context.m911_2.esus: In this sound: how bright the note stays while you hold it.
context.m902_1.fixed_cv: In this sound: 0, so only the envelope opens the amplifier. Turn it up and the note never stops.

tweaks.try: Turn T2 on the second 911 down to 4
tweaks.hear: A short, plucky blip of brightness at the start of each note.
A whistling peak that sweeps down with each note.

sounds.name: Expressive Lead #1
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 15 guide
sounds.blurb: Two sawtooth oscillators through the ladder filter, with a vibrato that fades in only on held notes.
sounds.how: The guide’s first lead. Two linked 921Bs are mixed into the 904A and a 902 under the first 911. The vibrato is the clever part: the 921, running slowly, goes through the second 902, and the second 911 opens that amplifier with a long T1. So each held note starts steady and the vibrato fades in; play legato and the second envelope never restarts.

steps.title: Two linked oscillators from the keyboard
steps.why:
The keyboard drives the 921A, the 921A drives the first 921B, and the second 921B is chained from the first.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A FREQUENCY IN 1, 921A FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ, 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ.
- 921B (2) FREQUENCY +0.1: a hair sharp, so the two beat slowly.

steps.title: Mixer, filter, amplifier
steps.why:
Both sawtooths into the CP3A-M, the mix into the 904A, the 904A into the first 902, and that to the output.
- Cables: both SAWTOOTH outputs to CP3A-M INPUT 1 and 2, then CP3A-M OUTPUT + to 904A SIG IN, 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1), 902 (1) to OUTPUT.
- CP3A-M GAIN 1 and 2 at 6, MASTER 8.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 1.5, REGENERATION 2.
- Not heard yet: the 902 is shut until an envelope opens it.

steps.title: Triggers and the loudness envelope
steps.why:
The CM1A’s TRIG goes into a CP35 multiple so it can fire both 911s. The first opens the first 902.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG to CP35 MULTIPLE A, then MULTIPLE A 1 and 2 to the two 911 S-TRIG INs, 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- 911 (1): T1 3, T2 6, E SUS 8, T3 6.
- Listen for: a warm, steady lead.

steps.title: A vibrato that waits
steps.why:
The 921 runs as an LFO. Its AUX output goes through the second 902, which the second 911 opens slowly, and the result goes to both oscillators’ DC MOD through CP35 MULTIPLE B.
- 921 COARSE RNG on SUB, FREQUENCY +1 (about 5 Hz), AUX OUT WAVEFORM sine, AUX OUT LEVEL 2.2.
- 911 (2): T1 8 (about 2 seconds), E SUS 10, T3 4.
- Cables: 921 AUX OUT 1 to 902 (2) SIG IN +, 902 (2) SIG OUT + to CP35 MULTIPLE B, MULTIPLE B 1 and 2 to the two DC MODs, 911 (2) OUT to 902 (2) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: hold a note and the vibrato swells in after a second or so.

context.m921.aux_level: In this sound: the vibrato depth. Small moves make a big difference, because every volt is an octave.
context.m921.frequency: In this sound: the vibrato speed.
context.m911_2.t1: In this sound: how long the vibrato takes to fade in.
context.m921b_2.frequency: In this sound: the detune between the two oscillators, which gives the slow beating.
context.m904a.fixed_cv: In this sound: the brightness of the lead.

tweaks.try: Turn T1 on the second 911 down to 3
tweaks.hear: The vibrato is there from the start of every note.
The two oscillators now play a fifth apart.

sounds.name: Expressive Lead #2
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 15 guide
sounds.blurb: Two rectangular waves with slowly moving pulse width, one detuned, through the filter with its own envelope.
sounds.how: The guide’s second lead uses pulse-width modulation. The 921, as a slow LFO, moves the 921A’s WIDTH input, and the 921A passes that on to both linked 921Bs. As each rectangular wave gets thinner and wider its tone changes, and with the second oscillator a little detuned the two shimmer like a chorus. The second 911 sweeps the 904A on each note.

steps.title: Two linked oscillators, pitch and width
steps.why:
Pitch and width both come from the 921A, and both chain on to the second 921B.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A FREQUENCY and WIDTH TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ and LINK WIDTH; then both link jacks on to 921B (2).
- 921B (2) FREQUENCY +0.12.
- 921A WIDTH 5 (50 %).

steps.title: Rectangular waves into the voice
steps.why:
Both RECTANGULAR outputs into the mixer, then the filter and amplifier as usual, with both envelopes.
- CP3A-M GAIN 1 and 2 at 6, MASTER 8.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −1, REGENERATION 2.
- 911 (1): T1 2, T2 6, E SUS 8, T3 5.5. 911 (2): T1 4, T2 6, E SUS 4, T3 5.5.
- Listen for: a hollow, reedy lead with a soft filter sweep.

steps.title: The 921 moves the width
steps.why:
The 921, as a slow LFO, goes through CP35 attenuator 1 into the 921A’s WIDTH input, so both pulse widths swing together.
- 921 COARSE RNG on SUB, FREQUENCY −0.5 (under 2 Hz).
- CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 at 2.5: about ±20 % of width.
- Cables: 921 SINE to CP35 IN 1, CP35 OUT 1 to 921A WIDTH IN 1.
- Listen for: a slow, chorus-like movement in the tone.

context.cp35.att1: In this sound: the depth of the width sweep. Past about 3.5 the width goes beyond the ends and the wave drops out for part of each sweep.
context.m921.frequency: In this sound: the speed of the shimmer.
context.m921a_1.width: In this sound: the centre of the width sweep.
context.m921b_2.frequency: In this sound: the detune of the second oscillator.

tweaks.hear: The shimmer stops: a plain, static square wave.

sounds.name: Space Rock
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 15 guide
sounds.blurb: A whistling self-oscillating filter swept by two slow oscillators, over wind made from pink noise.
sounds.how: Two classic space-rock sounds at once, and neither uses the keyboard. The 904A with REGENERATION near the top rings on its own as a sine wave, and the slow 921 and the first 921B (in its LO range) move its pitch. Pink noise through the 904B high-pass, swept by the second 921B, makes the wind. Both go through the mixer to the output.

steps.title: The filter sings on its own
steps.why:
With REGENERATION at 9.5 the 904A oscillates with nothing at its input. The mixer takes it to the output.
- 904A REGENERATION 9.5, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −2, so the sweeps swing round a low whistle.
- Cables: 904A SIG OUT to CP3A-M INPUT 1, CP3A-M OUTPUT + to OUTPUT.
- CP3A-M GAIN 1 at 5, MASTER 8.
- Listen for: a pure, steady whistle.

steps.title: Two slow sweeps
steps.why:
The 921 (on SUB) and the first 921B (on LO) both move the filter’s pitch, at different speeds, so the whistle wanders.
- 921 COARSE RNG on SUB, FREQUENCY −2.
- 921B (1) RANGE LO. The 921A sets its speed: FREQUENCY −6 on OCTAVE.
- Cables: 921 SINE to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1, 921A FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ, 921B (1) SINE to 904A CONTROL INPUT 2.
- Listen for: a swooping, warbling whistle.

steps.title: Wind
steps.why:
Pink noise through the 904B high-pass, swept by the second 921B (also on LO, chained from the first).
- Cables: 923 PINK NOISE 1 to 904B SIG IN, 904B SIG OUT to CP3A-M INPUT 2, 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ, 921B (2) SINE to 904B CONTROL INPUT 1.
- 921B (2) RANGE LO, FREQUENCY +5 (a different speed).
- 904B FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 1. CP3A-M GAIN 2 at 6.
- Listen for: rushing wind behind the whistle.

context.m904a.regeneration: In this sound: at 9.5 the filter is the sound source. Below about 9 it falls silent, because nothing is going into it.
context.m921.frequency: In this sound: the speed of one of the two sweeps.
context.m904b.fixed_cv: In this sound: how thin the wind is.
context.cp3am_1.gain2: In this sound: the level of the wind against the whistle.

tweaks.try: Turn the 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE up to 3
tweaks.hear: The whistle moves up into a shrill, piercing range.
The wind gusts much more slowly.

sounds.name: Percussive Lead
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 15 guide
sounds.blurb: A triangle and a detuned sawtooth with a hard front and a filter that keeps moving: made for fast melodic lines.
sounds.how: The guide’s percussive lead. The first 911 gives the amplifier an instant attack and a short fall to a low sustain, so each note has a hard front. The second 911 opens the filter slowly and lets it go over seconds, and the slow 921 adds a gentle sweep on top, so a repeated pattern never sounds quite the same twice.

steps.title: Triangle and sawtooth
steps.why:
Two linked 921Bs: the first’s TRIANGLE and the second’s SAWTOOTH into the mixer, then the usual filter and amplifier.
- Cables: the keyboard to the 921A and both 921Bs; TRIANGLE (1) to CP3A-M INPUT 1, SAWTOOTH (2) to INPUT 2; CP3A-M to 904A to 902 (1) to OUTPUT.
- 921B (2) FREQUENCY +0.08: slightly detuned.
- CP3A-M GAIN 1 at 7, GAIN 2 at 5, MASTER 8.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −1, REGENERATION 3.

steps.title: A hard front
steps.why:
The first 911 on the amplifier: no attack, a short fall to a low sustain.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG through CP35 MULTIPLE A to both 911s; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- 911 (1): T1 0, T2 5.4 (200 ms), E SUS 4, T3 5.4.
- Listen for: notes that start with a click of energy and drop back.

steps.title: Slow filter movement
steps.why:
The second 911 opens the filter over about a second and lets it go over four; the 921, as a slow LFO, sways it as well, through CP35 attenuator 1.
- 911 (2): T1 7.3, T2 3.8, E SUS 9, T3 8.9.
- 921 COARSE RNG on SUB, FREQUENCY −1. CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 at 1.5.
- Cables: 911 (2) OUT to 904A CONTROL INPUT 2; 921 SINE to CP35 IN 1, CP35 OUT 1 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: the line gets brighter the longer you keep playing, and breathes slowly.

context.m911_1.esus: In this sound: how much of each note is left after the hard front.
context.m911_2.t1: In this sound: how slowly the filter opens, so a run of notes brightens as it goes.
context.cp35.att1: In this sound: how far the 921 sways the filter.
context.m904a.regeneration: In this sound: a little resonance for bite.

tweaks.try: Turn E SUS on the first 911 down to 0
tweaks.hear: Every note becomes a short pluck.

tweaks.try: Turn T1 on the second 911 down to 3
tweaks.hear: The filter snaps open on each note instead of building up.

sounds.name: Ladder Bass
sounds.ref: The classic modular bass
sounds.blurb: Two oscillators an octave apart through the ladder filter, with a snappy filter envelope and key tracking.
sounds.how: A sawtooth at 8’ and a rectangular wave an octave below at 16’ give a deep, solid base. The 904A is closed well down and the second 911 snaps it open on each note, which gives the round “thump”. The CM1A’s second CV goes to the filter too, so high notes are as bright as low ones. The 902 is set to EXP, which makes the loudness envelope snappier.

steps.title: Two oscillators an octave apart
steps.why:
The first 921B’s SAWTOOTH at 8’ and the second’s RECTANGULAR an octave down at 16’, both from the keyboard.
- 921B (1) RANGE 8’, 921B (2) RANGE 16’.
- CP3A-M GAIN 1 at 7, GAIN 2 at 5, MASTER 8.
- Cables: the keyboard to both 921Bs; SAWTOOTH (1) to INPUT 1, RECTANGULAR (2) to INPUT 2; CP3A-M to 904A to 902 (1) to OUTPUT.

steps.title: Snappy envelopes
steps.why:
Both 911s with no attack. The first opens the 902 (on EXP), the second snaps the closed filter open.
- 902 (1) CONTROL MODE EXP.
- 911 (1): T1 0, T2 6, E SUS 9, T3 3.5 (on EXP the sustain needs to be high to be heard). 911 (2): T1 0, T2 5, E SUS 2, T3 3.5.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 3.
- Cables: the triggers to both 911s; 911 (1) to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1; 911 (2) to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: a round, punchy bass with a “thump” on each note.

steps.title: The filter follows the keys
steps.why:
The CM1A’s second CV goes to the filter as well, at 1 V per octave, so it opens by an octave for every octave you play.
- Cable: CM1A CV 2 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 2.
- Listen for: the high notes of the riff stay as bright as the low ones.

context.m904a.fixed_cv: In this sound: how dark the bass is under the thump.
context.m911_2.t2: In this sound: the length of the thump.
context.m902_1.mode: In this sound: EXP makes the loudness drop away faster after the start.
context.m904a.regeneration: In this sound: a little resonance gives the thump its “wow”.

tweaks.try: Turn T2 on the second 911 up to 6.5
tweaks.hear: A longer, slower “wow” on each note.

sounds.name: Sync Sweep
sounds.ref: Hard sync on a modular
sounds.blurb: One 921B hard-synced to the other, with an envelope sweeping its pitch: the tearing sync lead.
sounds.how: The second 921B is set to STRONG sync and fed the first one’s sawtooth, so it restarts on every cycle of the first and keeps that pitch. Raising its own frequency then changes only its tone, adding a vocal, tearing edge. The second 911, turned down through a CP35 attenuator, pushes its pitch up at the start of each note, so every note sweeps.

steps.title: Lock one oscillator to the other
steps.why:
Both 921Bs follow the keyboard. The first’s SAWTOOTH goes to the second’s SYNC IN, and only the second is heard.
- 921B (2) SYNC STRONG, FREQUENCY +5.
- Cables: the keyboard to both 921Bs; SAWTOOTH (1) to 921B (2) SYNC IN; SAWTOOTH (2) to CP3A-M INPUT 1; then the usual filter, amplifier and envelope on the 902.
- CP3A-M GAIN 1 at 7, MASTER 8. 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 3.
- 911 (1): T1 1, T2 6, E SUS 8, T3 5.
- Listen for: a bright, nasal tone at the first oscillator’s pitch.

steps.title: An envelope sweeps the synced pitch
steps.why:
The second 911 goes through CP35 attenuator 1 to the second 921B’s DC MOD. Each note starts with its pitch high and falls back, so the tone sweeps.
- 911 (2): T1 0, T2 6.5, E SUS 2, T3 5.
- CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 at 3: up to about 1.8 V, nearly two octaves.
- Cables: 911 (2) OUT to CP35 IN 1, CP35 OUT 1 to 921B (2) DC MOD.
- Listen for: a tearing “yow” at the start of every note.

context.m921b_2.frequency: In this sound: the tone of the synced oscillator, not its pitch. Sweep it and listen to the harmonics move.
context.m921b_2.sync: In this sound: STRONG locks it. Try OFF to hear the two oscillators drift apart.
context.cp35.att1: In this sound: how far the envelope sweeps the synced pitch.
context.m911_2.t2: In this sound: how long the sweep takes.

tweaks.try: Switch SYNC on the second 921B to OFF
tweaks.hear: The sweep becomes an ordinary pitch bend at the start of each note.

sounds.name: Talking Filter Bank
sounds.ref: The 914 Fixed Filter Bank
sounds.blurb: Two oscillators through the 914 with its bands set into an “ah” vowel, so every note sounds sung.
sounds.how: The 914 does not follow the note: its fourteen bands sit at fixed frequencies. That is what a voice does too: the shape of the mouth makes fixed peaks (formants) whatever note is sung. Here the bands round 700 Hz and 1 kHz are up, with a smaller peak near 2.8 kHz and the rest down, which is roughly the vowel “ah”. Play up and down and listen to the vowel stay put while the pitch moves.

steps.title: Into the filter bank, all bands open
steps.why:
A RECTANGULAR and a SAWTOOTH mixed and sent through the 914 instead of the 904A, then the 902 and its envelope.
- Cables: the keyboard to both 921Bs; RECTANGULAR (1) and SAWTOOTH (2) to the mixer; CP3A-M OUTPUT + to 914 INPUT 1; 914 OUTPUT 1 to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) to OUTPUT; CM1A TRIG to 911 (1); 911 (1) to 902 (1).
- CP3A-M GAIN 1 and 2 at 5, MASTER 7. 921B (2) FREQUENCY +0.1.
- 911 (1): T1 4, T2 7, E SUS 8, T3 6.
- Every 914 knob at 10: the bank is flat, so the sound is plain.

steps.title: Shape an “ah”
steps.why:
Peaks round 700 Hz and 1 kHz, a smaller one near 2.8 kHz, and the rest turned down.
- LOW PASS 3, 125 2, 175 2, 250 3, 350 5, 500 8, 700 10, 1000 10, 1400 6, 2000 3, 2800 7, 4000 3, 5600 1, HIGH PASS 0.
- Listen for: an open vowel that stays the same as the notes move.

context.m914.band_700: In this sound: the first vowel peak.
context.m914.band_1000: In this sound: the first vowel peak, with 700 Hz.
context.m914.band_2800: In this sound: the second, higher vowel peak.
context.m914.band_350: In this sound: turn this up and 700 down and the vowel closes towards “oh”.

tweaks.try: Turn 350 up to 10 and 1000 down to 3
Turn 2000 up to 10 and 700 down to 4

sounds.name: Ghost Wind
sounds.ref: Resonant noise
sounds.blurb: Pink noise through a ringing filter that the keyboard tunes, so the wind whistles your notes.
sounds.how: Noise has every frequency in it, so a resonant filter picks out a pitch from it: a whistle in the wind. With REGENERATION high the 904A rings at its cutoff, and the keyboard CV on a control input moves the cutoff an octave per octave, so the whistle plays your notes. The slow 921 sways it, and a 911 with long times swells it in and out.

steps.title: Noise through the filter
steps.why:
Pink noise into the 904A with high REGENERATION, then the 902 under a slow envelope.
- Cables: 923 PINK NOISE 1 to 904A SIG IN, 904A to 902 (1) to OUTPUT; CM1A TRIG to 911 (1), 911 (1) to 902 (1).
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 8.5.
- 911 (1): T1 7.5, T2 7, E SUS 9, T3 8.5.
- Listen for: a breathy whistle that swells in and fades.

steps.title: The keys tune the whistle
steps.why:
The CM1A CV goes straight to the filter’s cutoff, at 1 V per octave.
- Cable: CM1A CV 1 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: the whistle now follows the notes.

steps.title: A slow sway
steps.why:
The 921 on SUB, turned down through CP35 attenuator 1, wobbles the cutoff a little.
- 921 COARSE RNG on SUB, FREQUENCY −2. CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 at 0.4.
- Cables: 921 SINE to CP35 IN 1, CP35 OUT 1 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 2.
- Listen for: the whistle wavers like wind in a gap.

context.m904a.regeneration: In this sound: how pitched the wind is. Lower is more hiss; higher is more whistle.
context.m911_1.t1: In this sound: how slowly each gust swells in.
context.cp35.att1: In this sound: how far the whistle wavers.

sounds.name: Modular Brass
sounds.ref: In the style of Wendy Carlos — "Switched-On Bach"
sounds.blurb: Two detuned sawtooths with a filter that opens a little slower than the loudness: a bright, brassy swell.
sounds.how: Brass gets brighter as it gets louder. Here the second 911 opens the 904A over about 140 ms while the first opens the amplifier a little faster, so each note starts soft and blooms. The keyboard also moves the filter, so the tone is even across the range. The two sawtooths are a few cents apart for body.

steps.title: Two detuned sawtooths
steps.why:
Both 921B SAWTOOTH outputs mixed, the second a few cents sharp, through the usual voice.
- 921B (2) FREQUENCY +0.12.
- CP3A-M GAIN 1 and 2 at 6, MASTER 8.
- Cables: the keyboard to both 921Bs; both SAWTOOTHs to the mixer; CP3A-M to 904A to 902 (1) to OUTPUT.

steps.title: Loudness, then brightness
steps.why:
The first 911 opens the amplifier; the second opens the filter a little later and further.
- 911 (1): T1 3.5, T2 6, E SUS 8, T3 5.
- 911 (2): T1 5, T2 6.5, E SUS 5, T3 5.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −2, REGENERATION 1.
- Cables: triggers to both 911s; 911 (1) to 902 (1); 911 (2) to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: each note swells in and brightens: “bwah”.

steps.title: Even tone across the keys
steps.why:
CM1A CV 2 to the filter, so it tracks the notes.
- Cable: CM1A CV 2 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 2.

context.m911_2.t1: In this sound: how slowly the brightness blooms. Longer is softer and more like a horn section.
context.m911_2.esus: In this sound: how bright a held note stays.
context.m921b_2.frequency: In this sound: the detune that gives the section its body.

tweaks.try: Turn T1 on the second 911 up to 6.5
Turn the 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE up to 0

sounds.name: Clangy Bell
sounds.ref: Audio-rate FM between two oscillators
sounds.blurb: The 921 at audio rate shaking a 921B’s pitch through AC MOD: metallic, bell-like overtones that ring away.
sounds.how: Frequency modulation at audio rate does not sound like vibrato: it adds new overtones. When the two oscillators are at an odd ratio the overtones do not line up with the harmonic series, and the result is a bell or a gong. Both oscillators follow the keyboard (the 921 from CM1A CV 2), so the ratio, and with it the bell’s character, stays the same in every key. A 902 on EXP with a long T2 makes the strike and ring.

steps.title: A pure sine, struck
steps.why:
The first 921B’s SINE straight into the 902, with a percussive envelope.
- Cables: the keyboard to the 921A and 921B (1); SINE (1) to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) to OUTPUT; CM1A TRIG to 911 (1); 911 (1) to 902 (1).
- 902 (1) CONTROL MODE EXP.
- 911 (1): T1 0, T2 8, E SUS 0, T3 7.5.
- Listen for: a soft, struck sine, like a tuning fork.

steps.title: The 921 at an odd ratio
steps.why:
The 921 in its audio range, following the keys and tuned 7.9 semitones above the 921B at 4’, goes through CP35 attenuator 1 into the 921B’s AC MOD.

sounds.name: Upside-Down Trigger
sounds.ref: S-triggers and V-triggers
sounds.blurb: A lesson in Moog triggers: what a V-trigger does to a 911, and the two ways to put it right.
sounds.how: Moog envelopes are fired by an S-trigger: a line pulled down to 0 V while a key is held. Most other gear sends a V-trigger: +5 V while the key is held. Patch a V-trigger into a 911 and it reads “key held” when nothing is played, and “let go” when you press a key, so the sound plays backwards. The CM1A can send either kind (TRIG MODE), and the 961 converts one into the other.

steps.title: A V-trigger into an S-trigger input
steps.why:
The usual voice, but with the CM1A set to send V-triggers.
- CM1A TRIG MODE on V-TRIG.
- Cables: the keyboard to the 921A and 921B (1); SAWTOOTH (1) to 904A SIG IN; 904A to 902 (1) to OUTPUT; CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) to 902 (1).
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 2. 911 (1): T1 3, T2 6, E SUS 8, T3 6.
- Listen for: sound between the notes, and silence fading in while each key is held. It is upside down.

steps.title: Fix one: switch the CM1A to S-TRIG
steps.why:
The CM1A sends the kind of trigger the 911 expects.
- CM1A TRIG MODE on S-TRIG.
- Listen for: ordinary notes again.

steps.title: Fix two: the 961 converts
steps.why:
With TRIG MODE on BOTH the upper TRIG is an S-trigger and the lower a V-trigger. The lower one goes through the 961 (V-TRIG IN A to S-TRIG OUT) to fire the second 911, which sweeps the filter.
- CM1A TRIG MODE on BOTH.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG (lower) to 961 V-TRIG IN A (left) 1; 961 S-TRIG OUT (left) to 911 (2) S-TRIG IN; 911 (2) OUT to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −1. 911 (2): T1 2, T2 5.5, E SUS 3, T3 5.
- Listen for: both envelopes the right way up: notes with a filter sweep.

context.cm1a.trig_mode: In this sound: the whole lesson. V-TRIG plays it upside down; S-TRIG and BOTH play it the right way up.
context.m911_1.t1: In this sound: with the trigger upside down you hear this as the fade-in after each key is let go.

sounds.name: Singing Filter
sounds.ref: The 904A as an oscillator
sounds.blurb: No oscillator at all: the 904A rings on its own as a sine wave, played from the keyboard.
sounds.how: At full REGENERATION the 904A whistles at its cutoff frequency with nothing at its input. Its cutoff responds at 1 V per octave, the same as the oscillators, so the CM1A CV on a control input plays it in tune. A 911 on a 902 makes notes, and the 921, turned well down, adds a vibrato. It is a pure, flute-like tone.

steps.title: The filter rings

- 904A REGENERATION 10, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) to OUTPUT; CM1A TRIG to 911 (1); 911 (1) to 902 (1).
- 911 (1): T1 3.5, T2 6, E SUS 9, T3 6.
- Listen for: a pure whistle that plays the notes. If it is out of tune, nudge FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE.

- Cable: 921 AUX OUT 1 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 2.
- Listen for: a gentle, flute-like wobble.

sounds.name: Boogie Octave Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Kashif — Brooklyn boogie, early 1980s
sounds.blurb: A buzzy sawtooth with a square wave an octave under it, popped open by the ladder filter on every note.
sounds.how: One 921A drives both 921Bs, so a single keyboard cable plays two oscillators: the first at 8’ for the buzz, the second at 16’ for the weight. They meet in the CP3A-M, go through the 904A and out of the 902. The second 911 is turned down through a CP35 attenuator before it reaches the filter, so the pop is bright but not shrill. The two envelopes are fired from the CM1A’s two TRIG jacks, which both give S-triggers on S-TRIG.

sounds.name: Width-Snap Funk Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Slave — Dayton synth funk, 1980
sounds.blurb: A pulse bass whose width snaps from hollow to thin on every note: a rubbery funk “thwack”.
sounds.how: The 921A does more than tune its 921Bs: it also sends them a width voltage. Here an envelope is patched into the 921A’s WIDTH IN 1, so each note starts as a near-square and narrows in a fraction of a second. That moving width is a tone change the filter cannot make, and it is the snap in the sound. The 921A’s WIDTH TO 921B jack has to be patched to the 921B’s LINK WIDTH, or the rectangular wave stays square.

steps.title: A narrow pulse from the 921A
steps.why:
The keyboard drives the 921A and the 921A drives the first 921B, pitch and width both. Its RECTANGULAR goes straight into the 904A, no mixer needed.
- 921B (1) RANGE 8’.
- 921A (1) WIDTH 1 · 18 %.
- 904A: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 2.5, REGENERATION 2.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 5 · 140 ms, E SUS 7 · 3.9 V, T3 2.5 · 17 ms.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921A (1) WIDTH TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK WIDTH; 921B (1) RECTANGULAR to 904A SIG IN; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.

The second 911 goes through CP35 attenuator 1 to the 921A’s WIDTH IN 1. At its peak it adds about 2.4 V, widening the pulse from 18 % to about 56 %; as it decays the pulse narrows again.

- Cables: CM1A TRIG (lower) to 911 (2) S-TRIG IN; 911 (2) OUT to CP35 IN 1; CP35 OUT 1 to 921A (1) WIDTH IN 1.

sounds.name: Ladder Acid Line
sounds.ref: In the style of DJ Pierre — Chicago acid house, 1987
sounds.blurb: One sawtooth through the ladder filter turned up near its whistle, squelching on every sixteenth.
sounds.how: Acid is a bass line through a resonant low-pass whose cutoff jumps with each note. The 904A’s REGENERATION is high, so the cutoff becomes a peak you can hear; the second 911 kicks it open and lets it fall back, and the CM1A’s second CV makes the peak follow the notes, so the octave jumps squeal in tune.

sounds.name: Inverted Squelch
sounds.ref: In the style of Adonis — “No Way Back”, Chicago, 1986
sounds.blurb: A bass whose filter starts shut and swells open on every note: a squelch played backwards.
sounds.how: A 911 can only rise and fall, but a 902 can turn it upside down. Here the second 911 goes into 902 (2), held open by its FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE, and its SIG OUT − gives the envelope inverted. In the 904A’s CONTROL INPUT 1 that pulls the cutoff six octaves down at the start of each note, then lets it climb back to the bright FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE as the envelope decays: an “ooo-WAH” instead of a “yow”.

sounds.name: Deep House Sub
sounds.ref: In the style of Kerri Chandler — New Jersey deep house, 1990s
sounds.blurb: A round sine sub with a soft knock on top, shaped by the fixed filter bank instead of the ladder.
sounds.how: The 914 is twelve fixed band-pass filters with a low-pass and a high-pass at either end. Turned down above 250 Hz it is a tone control no ladder can be: the bottom stays full, the mids go, and a little of the 1400 and 2000 Hz bands is kept so the bass still knocks on small speakers. A sine and a triangle give it next to nothing to remove, so what is left is warm and deep.

steps.why:
The first 921B’s SINE for the sub, the second’s TRIANGLE for a little edge, mixed into the 914 and from there to the 902.

- 921B (2) RANGE 8’.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 8, GAIN 2 4, MASTER GAIN 8.

sounds.name: Hi-NRG Octave Pump
sounds.ref: In the style of Patrick Cowley — “Menergy”, San Francisco, 1981
sounds.blurb: Driving octave eighths from three oscillators: two 921Bs and the 921 underneath as a sine sub.
sounds.how: The System 15 has three audio oscillators if you want them: the two 921Bs and the 921. The Default patch already sends the keyboard to the 921’s FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1, so it follows the riff; on AUDIO and 16’ its SINE is a sub an octave under the 921Bs. Mixed with a sawtooth and a slightly sharp rectangular wave, it gives the full, pumping bass of early hi-NRG.

sounds.name: Sync Yow Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of The System — “You Are in My System”, New York, 1982
sounds.blurb: A synced 921B swept by an envelope: a vocal “yow” at the start of every bass note.
sounds.how: With SYNC on STRONG, the second 921B restarts its cycle each time the first one’s sawtooth resets, so it stays at the first one’s pitch whatever its own tuning. Raising its own pitch then changes only the tone. An envelope into its DC MOD raises it at the start of each note and lets it fall back, so the harmonics sweep down: a talking bass with no filter sweep at all.

sounds.name: FM Wobble Growl
sounds.ref: In the style of Kode9 — London dubstep, mid-2000s
sounds.blurb: A sine sub that growls in time: one 921B frequency-modulates the other, and a 902 opens and shuts the FM.
sounds.how: The two 921Bs both follow the keys, so the second one’s SINE into the first one’s AC MOD is frequency modulation at a 1:1 ratio: it adds harmonics in tune with the note. Instead of patching it straight in, it goes through 902 (2), used as a modulation amplifier, and the 921 on SUB opens and shuts that 902 at an eighth-note rate. The FM depth, not the filter, makes the wobble.

sounds.name: Berlin Ladder Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Michael Hoenig — “Departure from the Northern Wasteland”, Berlin, 1978
sounds.blurb: A rolling sixteenth-note sequence through a resonant ladder, with an LFO sweeping its cutoff slowly over the bars.
sounds.how: The Berlin-school sequence is a short, repeating figure whose tone moves while the notes stay the same. The 904A does the moving: the second 911 gives each note a bite, and the 921 on SUB, far below audio, slowly raises and lowers the whole cutoff through CP35 attenuator 2. Two 921Bs a tenth of a semitone apart thicken the line.

sounds.name: Breathing Width Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Redshift — British Berlin-school, late 1990s
sounds.blurb: Two pulse waves an octave apart whose width breathes together, under a dark three-against-four figure.
sounds.how: The 921A sends one width voltage to every linked 921B: the first takes it from the 921A’s WIDTH TO 921B, the second from the first one’s LINK WIDTH (to next). A slow LFO into the 921A’s WIDTH IN 1 therefore modulates both pulses at once, and they swell and thin together. The riff groups its sixteenths in threes against the four-beat bar, so it turns over as it loops.

sounds.name: Clamped Ratchet
sounds.ref: In the style of Conrad Schnitzler — “Con”, Berlin, 1978
sounds.blurb: Long held notes chopped into sixteenths by the 921, its rhythm restarted on every key press.
sounds.how: Here the 921 is a clock. Its RECTANGULAR on SUB, at the speed of sixteenths at this tempo, goes into the 961 interface, which turns each high half into an S-trigger for the first 911. That envelope chops the sound in 902 (1); the second 911, from the keyboard, holds 902 (2) open only while a key is down. The CM1A’s TRIG into the 921’s TRIG S jumps the LFO to its CLAMPING POINT on every note, so each ratchet starts on the beat.

steps.why:

- 921B (2) RANGE 4’.

sounds.name: Band-Pass Bleeps
sounds.ref: In the style of Cybotron — “Clear”, Detroit electro, 1983
sounds.blurb: Short, vocal bleeps from a narrow pulse through the high-pass and the ladder in series, both following the keys.
sounds.how: The 904B and 904A in series make a band-pass: with the high-pass at about 250 Hz and the resonant low-pass two octaves above, only a narrow band is left, which gives the bleeps their talking quality. To keep that band in the same place relative to each note, the keyboard CV has to reach both filters, so CM1A CV 2 goes into a CP35 MULTIPLE and from there to each.

sounds.name: Fixed-Ratio FM Glitch

sounds.blurb: A 7/8 figure where every note has a different metallic colour, from a modulator that ignores the keyboard.

Then the FM goes through 902 (2), opened by the second 911, so each note starts bright and settles toward a pure sine.

sounds.name: Glass Arp
sounds.ref: In the style of Bochum Welt — Italian IDM, 2000s
sounds.blurb: A delicate, ringing arpeggio with its body scooped away by the filter bank, leaving glass.
sounds.how: A triangle and a sine an octave up are already soft; the 914 then removes almost everything below 350 Hz, so what is left is the airy upper part of each note. With a long T2 and T3 on the first 911 the notes ring into each other’s space. It is a filter bank used as an EQ, which is how most studio owners used theirs.

sounds.name: Neon Width Arp
sounds.ref: In the style of Timecop1983 — Dutch synthwave, 2010s
sounds.blurb: A soft, detuned pulse arpeggio whose width follows the notes, with the filter breathing slowly.
sounds.how: The keyboard CV does not have to go to pitch. The CM1A’s second CV here goes to the 921A’s WIDTH IN 1, so the pulse grows wider as the arp climbs and thinner as it falls: the timbre moves with the melody. Two 921Bs, linked for pitch and width and a little apart, give the chorus, and the 921 slowly moves the ladder.

sounds.name: Ever New Sine Arp
sounds.ref: In the style of Beverly Glenn-Copeland — “Keyboard Fantasies”, 1986
sounds.blurb: A warm sine-and-triangle arpeggio whose vibrato fades in only on the longer notes.
sounds.how: A delayed vibrato needs an amplifier on the modulation. The 921’s AUX OUT, at a very small level, goes into 902 (2), and the second 911, with a slow attack, opens that 902: short notes pass before it opens, held notes start straight and then begin to sing. The output goes into the 921A’s FREQUENCY IN 2, so both 921Bs share it.

sounds.name: Ringing Ladder Arp

A sine two octaves up from the second 921B, very quiet, adds a high glint.

sounds.name: Bubble Ping Arp
sounds.ref: In the style of Haruomi Hosono — “Philharmony”, Tokyo, 1982
sounds.blurb: Playful, water-drop arps: a quiet triangle pinging a resonant ladder whose cutoff falls on every note.
sounds.how: At high REGENERATION the 904A rings at its cutoff. A short envelope that drops the cutoff quickly turns that ring into a falling “bloop”, like a drop of water. Keyboard tracking makes every bloop start at a pitch related to its note, so the arp stays musical.

sounds.name: Filmi Disco Arp

sounds.how: Hindi film disco took the European arp and played it in its own scales: here a figure with a flattened second and raised third (the Phrygian-dominant colour of many filmi songs). A sawtooth at 8’ with a square wave an octave up gives the bright, cutting tone that sits over strings and tabla.

sounds.name: Thirteen-Sixteen Machine Pulse
sounds.ref: In the style of Brad Fiedel — “The Terminator”, 1984
sounds.blurb: A metallic, limping pulse in 13/16, its clang from the 921 modulating a 921B at a tritone ratio.
sounds.how: The 921 is left on its Default-patch keyboard cable and on AUDIO, but set a tritone above an octave up: an irrational ratio, so its FM into the 921B’s AC MOD makes clanging, inharmonic overtones that keep the same character on every note. The 902 on EXP makes each hit fall away fast, like struck metal. The riff is four bars of 13/16, an off-kilter machine.

sounds.name: Chip Triplet Arp
sounds.ref: In the style of Hirokazu Tanaka — Nintendo game music, mid-1980s
sounds.blurb: A fast triplet arpeggio in a pure square wave, with a soft triangle bass doubling it two octaves down.
sounds.how: Game consoles of the 1980s had a couple of pulse voices and a triangle, and their composers faked chords with fast arpeggios. The first 921B’s RECTANGULAR, square with nothing in its width link, plays the arp straight into the 902 with no filter; the second 921B’s TRIANGLE two octaves down (32’) stands in for the console’s triangle channel.

sounds.name: Dead of Night Sync Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Eddie Jobson — U.K., “In the Dead of Night”, 1978
sounds.blurb: A biting, tearing sync lead whose tone sweeps slowly up and down under a fast prog line.
sounds.how: The second 921B is hard-synced to the first, so it keeps the first one’s pitch and its own tuning becomes tone. Rather than an envelope, the 921 on SUB sweeps that tuning slowly through CP35 attenuator 1 into the second 921B’s DC MOD, so the tearing quality rises and falls across the phrase, the way a player would ride a knob.

sounds.name: Synergy Brass Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Larry Fast — Synergy, “Electronic Realizations for Rock Orchestra”, 1975
sounds.blurb: A big, brassy fanfare lead: two sawtooths through a slowly opening ladder, then shaped by the filter bank.
sounds.how: Brass needs a filter that opens a little after the note starts, so the second 911 has a slow T1. The 914 after the 904A is the part a single synth cannot do: with the low bands turned down and the 2800–5600 Hz region trimmed, it carves fixed resonances like the bell of a horn, which stay put whatever note is played.

sounds.name: Sound-Chaser FM Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Patrick Moraz — Yes, “Sound Chaser”, 1974
sounds.blurb: A lead that starts clean and turns gnarled as each note is held, the FM fading in through a 902.
sounds.how: The 921 on AUDIO stays on the keyboard (its Default-patch cable), tuned a fifth up, and its SAWTOOTH frequency-modulates the first 921B. Instead of a fixed amount, the FM passes through 902 (2), and the second 911, with a slow T1, opens it: fast notes stay clean, held notes grow a snarling edge. That is what an amplifier on a modulation path is for.

sounds.name: Fusion Pulse Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Casiopea — Tokyo jazz-fusion, “Asayake”, 1979
sounds.blurb: A lively pulse lead with fast width modulation and vibrato, both from the one LFO.
sounds.how: The 921 is one LFO with several outputs at once. Its TRIANGLE, through CP35 attenuator 1, sweeps the 921A’s width quickly for a shimmering, chorus-like pulse; its AUX OUT, the same wave at a much lower level set by the AUX OUT LEVEL knob, adds vibrato through the 921A’s FREQUENCY IN 2. Width and pitch move together, in step.

sounds.name: Scoop Jazz-Funk Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Patrice Rushen — Los Angeles jazz-funk, late 1970s
sounds.blurb: A soft, round lead that scoops up into each note from half an octave below, like a singer.
sounds.how: To scoop up into a note, the pitch has to start low and rise: an envelope upside down. 902 (2) does it: the second 911 goes into its SIG IN −, which inverts, and a low FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE makes it an attenuator as well, so at most half a volt below the note comes out. Into the 921A’s FREQUENCY IN 2 that is a quick slide up from six semitones under.

sounds.name: Funky Worm Squeal
sounds.ref: In the style of Junie Morrison — Ohio Players, “Funky Worm”, 1973
sounds.blurb: A high, squealing, nasal lead from a resonant ladder that follows the keys and kicks open on each note.
sounds.how: The squeal is resonance. The 904A’s REGENERATION is near 8, and its cutoff follows the keyboard through CM1A CV 2 so the peak stays close to each note’s harmonics; the second 911 then kicks it up and lets it fall, so every note whoops. Sawtooth and square together give the peak plenty to ring on.

sounds.name: C64 Pulse Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Rob Hubbard — Commodore 64 game music, mid-1980s
sounds.blurb: A thin, buzzing pulse lead whose width sweeps on a ramp, with quick vibrato: home-computer music on a modular.
sounds.how: The home computer sound chips swept their pulse width with a ramp, over and over, and added fast vibrato. Here the 921 does both from one LFO: its SAWTOOTH, a ramp, through CP35 attenuator 1 into the 921A’s WIDTH IN 1, and its AUX OUT as vibrato into the 921A’s FREQUENCY IN 2. No filter: the pulse goes from the mixer straight to the 902.

sounds.name: Giallo Weak-Sync Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Fabio Frizzi — Italian horror film scores, late 1970s
sounds.blurb: An eerie, wavering lead from two oscillators in weak sync, through a band-pass, with a slow, wide vibrato.
sounds.how: WEAK sync does not force the second 921B to restart on every cycle: it only nudges it when it is nearly there. Tuned a fraction of a semitone flat, it keeps catching and slipping, which gives an unstable, uneasy shimmer. The 904A and 904B in series narrow the sound to a thin, nasal band, and the 921’s TRIANGLE, through CP35 attenuator 1, adds a slow vibrato over a semitone wide.

steps.why:

- 921B (1) RANGE 8’.
- 921B (2): RANGE 8’, SYNC WEAK, FREQUENCY −0.3 · -0.3 st.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 4, GAIN 2 5, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 904A: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 3, REGENERATION 5.
- 911 (1): T1 3 · 26 ms, T2 6 · 330 ms, E SUS 9 · 5.0 V, T3 5 · 140 ms.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SAWTOOTH to CP35 MULTIPLE A (in); CP35 MULTIPLE A 1 to 921B (2) SYNC IN; CP35 MULTIPLE A 2 to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) SAWTOOTH to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 904A SIG IN; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: a slightly unstable, shimmering lead.

steps.title: The 904B after the ladder
steps.why:

sounds.name: Ah Choir Bank

sounds.blurb: A breathy, wordless “ah” choir: two sawtooths and a little breath, shaped into a vowel by the 914.

Pink noise in the 914’s second input passes the same formants, so the choir breathes, and a whisper of vibrato from the 921’s AUX OUT makes it sing.

sounds.name: Plainchant Organum

sounds.name: Vowel Morph Voice
sounds.ref: In the style of Meredith Monk — “Dolmen Music”, 1981
sounds.blurb: A wordless voice that slides slowly through its vowels, “aa” to “oo” to “ee” and back, on every held note.
sounds.how: The 914 gives a fixed vowel; to make it move, the 904B high-pass and the 904A low-pass are patched in series after it as a band-pass, and the 921 on SUB moves both cutoffs together through one multiple. The band sweeps across the 914’s formants, lighting first the low ones and then the high ones: the voice changes vowel while the pitch stays put.

sounds.name: Sighing Shoegaze Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of Slowdive — “Souvlaki”, 1993
sounds.blurb: A wide, warbling pad that darkens as each note is held and brightens again as it fades away, like a sigh.

The second 911 goes into 902 (2) with its FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE at 6, so 902 (2) passes it at full level, and its SIG OUT − turns it upside down. Into the 904A, that pulls the cutoff down as the note settles and lets it rise again during the release. A tiny, slow pitch drift from the 921 adds the bent-guitar warble.

sounds.name: Inter-Dimensional Shimmer
sounds.ref: In the style of Iasos — “Inter-Dimensional Music”, 1975
sounds.blurb: A pure, floating pad with a high halo two octaves up that trembles on its own while the body stays still.

sounds.name: Planetary Resonance Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of Michael Stearns — “Planetary Unfolding”, 1981
sounds.blurb: A vast, whistling chord of resonances that lights up one band after another over a deep sawtooth.

Keep only the octave bands up and feed in pink noise, and the noise rings at those pitches: a chord that comes from the filter, not an oscillator. A sawtooth an octave down goes into the 914’s second input, and the 904A after the bank, swept slowly by the 921, picks out the bands one after another.

sounds.name: Copia Brass Swell
sounds.ref: In the style of Eluvium — “Copia”, Portland, 2007
sounds.blurb: A soft brass choir that swells into each note: loud first, then bright, like horns heard from far off.
sounds.how: Two 911s give two different swells. The first, on the 902, brings the note in over about a second; the second, on the 904A, is slower still, so the tone keeps opening after it has reached full volume. That lag, loudness then brightness, is what makes it sound like distant brass rather than a synthesizer.

sounds.name: Singing Bowl
sounds.ref: In the style of the Himalayan singing bowl, struck and left to ring
sounds.blurb: A struck metal bowl: a pure tone that rings for seconds, wavering as two close partials beat, with a high overtone above.
sounds.how: A real bowl is never perfectly round, so its main tone is two nearly equal frequencies that beat. Two linked 921Bs a fifth of a semitone apart do just that, about three beats a second around middle C. Bowls are not tuned in harmonic overtones either: the 921, kept on AUDIO and on the keyboard (its Default-patch cable), is set an octave and five semitones up, about 2.7 times the note, which gives the metallic upper ring.

steps.why:

sounds.how: A hard-synced oscillator’s sine output is not a sine any more: restarted every cycle of the first 921B, it becomes a bright, glassy wave whose colour depends on its own tuning. The 921 moves that tuning slowly through the second 921B’s DC MOD, so the bells change metal over a few bars. The 902 on EXP gives a quick, bell-like fall.

steps.title: A synced sine
steps.why:
Both 921Bs from the 921A; the first one’s SAWTOOTH into the second’s SYNC IN, STRONG; the second, tuned up, its SINE into the 902 on EXP.
- 921B (1) RANGE 8’.
- 921B (2): RANGE 8’, SYNC STRONG, FREQUENCY 9 · +9 st.
- 902 (1) CONTROL MODE EXP.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 6 · 330 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 5.5 · 220 ms.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SAWTOOTH to 921B (2) SYNC IN; 921B (2) SINE to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: glassy, bell-like notes at the first oscillator’s pitch.

steps.title: The metal drifts
steps.why:
The 921 on SUB, slow; its TRIANGLE through CP35 attenuator 1 into the second 921B’s DC MOD.
- 921: COARSE RNG SUB, RANGE 8’, SCALE ±6 OCT, FREQUENCY −2.
- CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 1.5.
- Cables: 921 TRIANGLE to CP35 IN 1; CP35 OUT 1 to 921B (2) DC MOD.
- Listen for: the bells’ colour turning slowly from soft to bright.

sounds.name: Submerged Pulse
sounds.ref: In the style of Loscil — “Submers”, Vancouver, 2002
sounds.blurb: Muffled, deep-water pulses in dotted rhythm, as if heard through a submarine hull.
sounds.how: The 904A on its lowest range keeps only the bottom of a sine and triangle, and its REGENERATION adds a soft, round resonance. The second 911 knocks the filter open briefly on every note, so each pulse has a dull, sonar-like “bloop”. The 914, with everything above 500 Hz turned down, finishes the hull.

sounds.name: Sublime Loop Build
sounds.ref: In the style of The Field — “From Here We Go Sublime”, Stockholm, 2007
sounds.blurb: A shimmering, repeating sixteenth loop that slowly opens up as the chord is held, like a track building for minutes.
sounds.how: The build is a 911 used as a very slow control, not a note shape. The second 911, with T1 near its longest, takes about four seconds to rise; through CP35 attenuator 1 into the 904A it slowly opens the filter while the loop repeats underneath. The keyboard trigger is held through the whole loop (the notes are tied), so the envelope keeps climbing.

sounds.name: Bamboo Breath Flute
sounds.ref: In the style of Deuter — “Ecstasy”, 1979
sounds.blurb: A breathy bamboo flute whose slow vibrato only arrives as each long note is held.
sounds.how: The flute is a sine through a breathy 904A with pink noise in it. The vibrato comes from the second 921B, unlinked and on LO, so it runs slowly on its own; but it reaches the first 921B only through 902 (2), and the second 911 opens 902 (2) slowly. So the 902 is the player’s choice: each note starts straight, and the slow head-shake vibrato of a shakuhachi player swells in.

sounds.name: Cradle Song Ocarina
sounds.ref: In the style of a Welsh cradle song, “Suo Gân”
sounds.blurb: A soft, round ocarina with a feathery edge of air, singing a gentle lullaby in three.
sounds.how: An ocarina is nearly a pure tone with breath around it. A triangle through a gentle 904A gives the tone; the air is white noise through the 923’s high-pass, mixed in low, so it sits above the note like the rush of breath across the mouthpiece. A whisper of vibrato from the 921’s AUX OUT makes it sing.

sounds.name: 808 Boom Kick
sounds.ref: In the style of 1980s Miami bass — the long, tuned, pitch-dropping 808 boom
sounds.blurb: A deep, tuned sine boom that thumps in high and sinks to its note, ringing on for a second under the beat.
sounds.how: An 808 kick is a sine wave whose pitch falls fast at the start. Here the first 921B, played from the keyboard so every boom is tuned, gives the sine; the second 911, with no sustain, is turned down by a CP35 attenuator and patched into the 921B’s DC MOD, so each hit starts an octave and a half up and drops to the note in a tenth of a second. The first 911 lets the sine ring for over a second, as Miami bass records do.

steps.why:
The keyboard plays the first 921B through the 921A; its SINE goes through the 902, struck and left to ring.

- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: a soft, low sine note on every hit, without any punch yet.

sounds.name: Warehouse Kick
sounds.ref: In the style of Frankie Knuckles — Chicago house at the Warehouse, mid-1980s
sounds.blurb: A short, punchy four-on-the-floor kick: a sine that snaps down in pitch with a tick of noise on top.
sounds.how: One envelope does two jobs through a CP35 MULTIPLE: the second 911, very fast, drops the first 921B’s pitch through an attenuator and opens 902 (2) for a burst of high-passed white noise, the beater’s click. The sine itself, left unlinked at a fixed low pitch, goes through the first 902 with a short decay. The two 902s meet in the CP3A-M so the click can be set against the body.

steps.title: A fixed-pitch body
steps.why:
The first 921B with nothing in its LINK FREQ, so it sits at its RANGE and FREQUENCY whatever key is played; its SINE through the first 902 into mixer input 1.
- 921B (1): RANGE 32’, FREQUENCY 3 · +3 st.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 8, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 5.5 · 220 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 4 · 60 ms.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: 921B (1) SINE to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + from OUTPUT L (app).
- Listen for: a dull, short low thud on each beat.

steps.title: One envelope, two places
steps.why:
The second 911 into CP35 MULTIPLE A. One copy goes through attenuator 1 into the 921B’s DC MOD for the pitch snap; another opens 902 (2).
- 911 (2): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 3.5 · 39 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 3 · 26 ms.
- CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 4.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG (lower) to 911 (2) S-TRIG IN; 911 (2) OUT to CP35 MULTIPLE A (in); CP35 MULTIPLE A 1 to CP35 IN 1; CP35 OUT 1 to 921B (1) DC MOD; CP35 MULTIPLE A 2 to 902 (2) CONTROL INPUT 1.

sounds.name: Electro Snare
sounds.ref: In the style of Mantronix — “Fresh Is the Word”, New York electro, 1985
sounds.blurb: A drum-machine snare: two short tuned triangle tones for the shell and a hiss of filtered noise for the wires.
sounds.how: Drum-machine snares are two parts, so this one uses both 902s. The two 921Bs, unlinked and tuned to two shell modes, are mixed and pass the first 902 with a very short decay. White noise from the 923 goes through the 904B, which takes out its bottom, and 902 (2) on EXP with its own, slightly longer, envelope. The two 902s go to the two output jacks, which are summed.

sounds.name: Syndrum Tom Fill
sounds.ref: In the style of Cerrone — “Supernature”, Paris disco, 1977
sounds.blurb: Electronic toms that go “pew”: tuned sine drums falling in pitch, rolling down a disco fill.
sounds.how: The Syndrum was a sine oscillator with a pitch envelope, and so is this. The keyboard tunes the first 921B, so the fill rolls down from high toms to low; the second 911, through an attenuator into DC MOD, makes each hit start over an octave up and slide down for a third of a second, which is the downward sweep heard all over late-1970s disco.

sounds.name: Machine Hi-Hats
sounds.ref: In the style of Juan Atkins — Model 500, “No UFO’s”, Detroit, 1985
sounds.blurb: Ticking closed hi-hats and hissing open ones from the same patch: the length of each note decides which.
sounds.how: White noise through the 904B on HIGH, with its cutoff high up, leaves only the top: a hat. The trick is the first 911: a short T2 falls to a low E SUS, and T3 is very short. A short note is a closed tick; a held note sits at E SUS, a quieter open hiss, until the key is let go and T3 chokes it, as a drum machine chokes its open hat.

steps.title: Noise with no bottom
steps.why:
White noise from the 923 into the 904B on HIGH, cut high, and through the 902.
- 904B: FREQUENCY RANGE HIGH, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 2.
- 902 (1): CONTROL MODE LIN, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: WHITE NOISE 1 to 904B SIG IN; 904B SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app).
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: nothing yet: the 902 is shut until an envelope opens it.

steps.title: Closed or open
steps.why:
The first 911 with a short T2 down to a low E SUS and a very short T3.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 4 · 60 ms, E SUS 3 · 1.7 V, T3 3.5 · 39 ms.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: short notes ticking, the longer off-beat notes hissing open and choking off.

context.m911_1.esus: In this sound: how loud the open hat is. At 0 every hat is closed.
context.m904b.fixed_cv: In this sound: how thin and metallic the hats are.

sounds.name: Freestyle Cowbell
sounds.ref: In the style of 1980s Latin freestyle — the 808 cowbell over electro beats
sounds.blurb: The clanking two-tone drum-machine cowbell, playing a syncopated freestyle pattern.
sounds.how: The 808 makes its cowbell from two square waves at about 540 and 800 Hz, a clashing interval that sounds metallic. The two 921Bs, unlinked so they keep those pitches on every key, give the squares; the 904B takes away the bottom, and the 902 on EXP gives the fast drop and short tail of a struck bell.

steps.title: Two clashing squares
steps.why:
Both 921Bs unlinked, on 4’, about a fifth and a bit apart; their RECTANGULAR outputs mixed into the 904B high-pass.
- 921B (1): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 0.6 · +0.6 st.
- 921B (2): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 7.4 · +7.4 st.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 4, GAIN 2 4, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 904B: FREQUENCY RANGE LOW, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0.5.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: 921B (1) RECTANGULAR to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) RECTANGULAR to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 904B SIG IN.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: (not heard yet) a harsh two-note buzz, waiting at the filter for the 902.

steps.title: Struck
steps.why:
The 904B through the 902, on EXP, with a short decay.
- 902 (1): CONTROL MODE EXP, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 6 · 330 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 4 · 60 ms.
- Cables: 904B SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: a bright clank with a quick, metallic tail.

sounds.name: Rhythm-Box Claves
sounds.ref: In the style of Sly and the Family Stone — the Maestro Rhythm King on “There’s a Riot Goin’ On”, 1971
sounds.blurb: A dry, woody “tock” high up, every hit exactly the same, playing a clave pattern.
sounds.how: Claves are a high, short sine. The 921 reaches higher than the 921Bs, up to 1’, and has something they do not: TRIG S. With the CM1A’s lower TRIG patched there, every note restarts the sine at the CLAMPING POINT, so every hit begins at the same place in the wave and sounds identical, as a rhythm box does.

steps.title: A high sine from the 921
steps.why:
The 921 on AUDIO at 1’, a little above, unpatched from the keyboard so it keeps its pitch; its SINE through the 902 on EXP with a tiny decay.
- 921: COARSE RNG AUDIO, RANGE 1’, SCALE ±6 OCT, FREQUENCY 0.3.
- 902 (1): CONTROL MODE EXP, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 4 · 60 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 3 · 26 ms.
- Cables: 921 SINE to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug: CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: a high, short “tock”, each one a little different.

steps.title: Every hit the same
steps.why:
The CM1A’s lower TRIG into the 921’s TRIG S, with the CLAMPING POINT at the middle of the wave.
- 921 CLAMPING POINT 5 · 50 %.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG (lower) to 921 TRIG S.
- Listen for: every hit now identical: a dry machine clave.

sounds.name: Rhythm-Box Congas
sounds.ref: In the style of Timmy Thomas — “Why Can’t We Live Together”, Miami, 1972
sounds.blurb: Round, tuned conga hits ringing like a hand on a skin, in a tumbao pattern.
sounds.how: There is no oscillator here at all. The second 911 is patched straight into the 904A’s SIG IN: a 6 V blip a few milliseconds long, which knocks the filter, set close to ringing, into a short tuned ring at its cutoff. The keyboard moves the cutoff, so it tunes the drum. The first 902 stops each ring before the next.

steps.title: An envelope as the sound
steps.why:
The second 911, very short, into the 904A’s SIG IN; the 904A near self-oscillation.
- 904A: FREQUENCY RANGE 2, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 8.
- 911 (2): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 2 · 11 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 2 · 11 ms.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG (lower) to 911 (2) S-TRIG IN; 911 (2) OUT to 904A SIG IN.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: (not heard yet) the filter ringing each time it is knocked.

steps.title: Tuned by the keys
steps.why:
CM1A CV 2 into the 904A’s CONTROL INPUT 1, so the ring follows the note.
- Cables: CM1A CV 2 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: (not heard yet) the open tone, the higher slap and the lower note.

steps.title: Damped by the hand
steps.why:
The 904A through the 902, with a short decay.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 6 · 330 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 4.5 · 92 ms.
- Cables: 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.

sounds.name: Sunrise Timpani
sounds.ref: In the style of Richard Strauss — the timpani of “Also sprach Zarathustra”, 1896
sounds.blurb: Big orchestral kettledrums pounding between tonic and dominant, with a soft mallet thud and a ring that sags in pitch.
sounds.how: A timpani has a fundamental and a strong partial about a fifth and an octave up; the two 921Bs give them, mixed. The mallet is pink noise through the 923 low-pass, let through by 902 (2) for an instant. The same quick envelope, split by a CP35 MULTIPLE, nudges the 921A’s pitch up a little at the strike, as a struck drumhead goes sharp before it settles.

steps.title: A drum and its partial
steps.why:
Both 921Bs from the 921A: the first’s SINE, the second’s SINE a twelfth up, quieter, mixed into the first 902, which rings for seconds.
- 921B (1) RANGE 8’.
- 921B (2): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 7 · +7 st.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 7, GAIN 2 2, MASTER GAIN 7.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 8 · 1.8 s, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 7 · 780 ms.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SINE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) SINE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: a deep, ringing tone on every stroke.

steps.why:
The second 911 into CP35 MULTIPLE A. One copy opens 902 (2) on pink noise through the 923 low-pass, into mixer input 3; another, through attenuator 1, goes to the 921A’s FREQUENCY IN 2.
- 923 LOW PASS 4 · 158 Hz.

- CP3A-M (1) GAIN 3 6.
- CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 0.3.

sounds.name: Electronic Bongo Clock
sounds.ref: In the style of Raymond Scott — “Soothing Sounds for Baby” and his rhythm machines, 1963
sounds.blurb: Hold a key and a little machine plays bongos at that pitch by itself, lurching between two speeds.
sounds.how: The 921 on SUB is a clock: its RECTANGULAR wave goes into a 961 V-TRIG IN B, and every rise gives an S-trigger from the 961’s S-TRIG OUT that fires the second 911. That envelope knocks the ringing 904A, tuned by the keyboard. The first 921B, slowed to LO, swings the clock between two rates through the 921’s FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; the keyboard’s own 911 only holds the 902 open while a key is down.

steps.title: A clock from the 921
steps.why:
The 921 on SUB, its RECTANGULAR into the 961’s V-TRIG IN B (left) 1; the 961’s S-TRIG OUT (left) into the second 911’s S-TRIG IN.
- 921: COARSE RNG SUB, RANGE 8’, SCALE ±6 OCT, FREQUENCY 1.2, RECTANGULAR WIDTH 3 · 34 %.
- 961 SWITCH-ON TIME (left) 0 · 40 ms.
- 911 (2): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 2.5 · 17 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 2 · 11 ms.
- Cables: 921 RECTANGULAR to 961 V-TRIG IN B (left) 1; 961 S-TRIG OUT (left) to 911 (2) S-TRIG IN.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: (not heard yet) the second 911 firing about six times a second.

steps.title: Knock a ringing filter
steps.why:
The second 911 into the 904A’s SIG IN, CM1A CV 2 tuning it, the 904A through the 902; the first 911 holds the 902 open while a key is down.
- 904A: FREQUENCY RANGE 2, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 8.2.
- 911 (1): T1 0.5 · 3 ms, T2 3 · 26 ms, E SUS 10 · 5.5 V, T3 4 · 60 ms.
- Cables: 911 (2) OUT to 904A SIG IN; CM1A CV 2 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: a steady bongo roll at the pitch of the key.

steps.title: A lurch in the clock
steps.why:
The first 921B, unlinked, on LO: its RECTANGULAR through CP35 attenuator 1 into the 921’s FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1.
- 921B (1): RANGE LO, FREQUENCY 4 · +4 st.
- CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 1.
- Cables: 921B (1) RECTANGULAR to CP35 IN 1; CP35 OUT 1 to 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: the roll speeding up and slowing down every second or so, like a hand drummer.

sounds.name: Krell Circuit
sounds.ref: In the style of Louis and Bebe Barron — “Forbidden Planet”, 1956
sounds.blurb: A living circuit moaning and gurgling: a whistling filter wobbling and twisted by an audio-rate tone.
sounds.how: The 904A with its REGENERATION at the top rings on its own: nothing goes into SIG IN at all. The keyboard tunes it, the 921 on SUB wobbles it, and the first 921B, at an audio rate, frequency-modulates the filter’s cutoff through an attenuator, which turns its pure whistle into the clangorous, inharmonic moan of the Barrons’ circuits. A slow envelope lets each sound sigh in and die away.

steps.title: A filter as an oscillator
steps.why:
The 904A with REGENERATION at 10 and nothing at SIG IN; CM1A CV 2 tunes it; through the 902 with slow, sighing times.
- 904A: FREQUENCY RANGE 2, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 10.
- 911 (1): T1 6 · 330 ms, T2 8 · 1.8 s, E SUS 6 · 3.3 V, T3 8 · 1.8 s.
- Cables: CM1A CV 2 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: a pure, steady whistle.

steps.title: A wobble

The 921 on SUB, its TRIANGLE through CP35 attenuator 1 into the 904A’s CONTROL INPUT 2.
- 921: COARSE RNG SUB, RANGE 8’, SCALE ±6 OCT, FREQUENCY −0.5.
- CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 2.
- Cables: 921 TRIANGLE to CP35 IN 1; CP35 OUT 1 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 2.
- Listen for: the whistle swooping up and down twice a second.

steps.title: Audio-rate FM of the filter

- 921B (1) RANGE 16’.
- CP35 ATTENUATOR 2 1.5.
- Cables: 921B (1) SINE to CP35 IN 2; CP35 OUT 2 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 3.

sounds.name: Radiophonic Swoop
sounds.ref: In the style of Delia Derbyshire — the “Doctor Who” theme, BBC Radiophonic Workshop, 1963
sounds.blurb: Singing noise that swoops up and falls away like wind in a time tunnel, each swoop pitched by the keys.
sounds.how: White noise through the 904A with plenty of REGENERATION is noise with a whistle in it. The second 911, through an attenuator, sweeps that whistle up three octaves and back down for every note, and the keyboard sets where it starts; the 921’s AUX OUT, at a whisper, keeps it wavering. It is the hand-swept filtered-noise “whoosh” of the Radiophonic Workshop, done with voltages.

sounds.name: Slow Ocean Surf
sounds.ref: In the style of Irv Teibel — “Environments 1: Psychologically Ultimate Seashore”, 1969
sounds.blurb: Waves rolling in and drawing back every few seconds, brightening as they break.
sounds.how: Pink noise through the 904A is the sea. The 921, slowed on SUB to one cycle every few seconds, is the swell: its TRIANGLE raises and lowers the 902’s gain, and its AUX OUT opens the filter at the same time, so each wave gets louder and brighter together. The keyboard’s trigger, in the 921’s TRIG S, restarts the wave from its trough with every key.

- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.

sounds.name: Garden Warbler
sounds.ref: In the style of Olivier Messiaen — “Catalogue d’oiseaux”, 1958
sounds.blurb: Quick, bright bird chirps, a burst of them on every key, each one flicking down in pitch.
sounds.how: A chirp is a high sine that falls fast. The 921 on SUB clocks the 961 about eight times a second, and each pulse fires the second 911, which a CP35 MULTIPLE sends both to the first 921B’s DC MOD (the flick in pitch) and to the first 902 (the chirp’s loudness). The first 902 then feeds 902 (2), which the keyboard’s envelope opens: two amplifiers in series, one for each chirp and one for the phrase.

steps.why:
The keyboard plays the first 921B, two octaves up; its SINE into the first 902.
- 921B (1) RANGE 2’.

- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + from OUTPUT L (app); 911 (1) OUT from 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: (not heard yet) a high, pure tone.

- 961 SWITCH-ON TIME (left) 0 · 40 ms.
- 902 (1): CONTROL MODE LIN, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0.
- CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 2.
- 911 (2): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 3.5 · 39 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 2 · 11 ms.

- Listen for: (not heard yet) a stream of falling chirps.

sounds.name: Sound-System Dub Siren
sounds.ref: In the style of the Jamaican sound-system dub siren, from King Tubby’s era on
sounds.blurb: A wailing square-wave siren that starts fast and winds down, ready to fire over a dub breakdown.
sounds.how: A dub siren is an oscillator whose pitch is swept by an LFO, and whose LFO is itself swept. Here the 921 on SUB, its SAWTOOTH through an attenuator into the 921A, wails the pitch; the second 911 goes into the 921’s own FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1, so each note starts the siren racing and lets it slow down as the envelope falls. The 923 low-pass softens the square, like a cheap speaker.

sounds.name: Droid Chatter
sounds.ref: In the style of Ben Burtt — the voice of R2-D2, “Star Wars”, 1977
sounds.blurb: A chattering little robot: whistles that jump between pitches in quick, stepped patterns as you play.

sounds.name: Ring-Mod Robot Voice
sounds.ref: In the style of Brian Hodgson — the Daleks’ voices, BBC Radiophonic Workshop, 1963
sounds.blurb: A grating, chopped robot voice barking out syllables.
sounds.how: The Daleks were a voice ring-modulated by a 30 Hz tone. Here the first 921B’s sawtooth, shaped into a vowel by the 914, is the voice; the 921, on AUDIO but tuned down to about 30 Hz, goes straight into the 902’s CONTROL INPUT 2. A 902 does not stop at the speed of an envelope: fed an audio-rate wave, it chops the voice 30 times a second. The first 911 comes through an attenuator, so it only half-opens the 902 and the sine does the rest.

sounds.name: Golden-Ratio FM Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of John Chowning — “Stria”, Stanford, 1977
sounds.blurb: A slowly blooming, glassy drone whose inharmonic partials grow and fade as the modulation rises and falls.
sounds.how: Chowning built “Stria” on frequency modulation at the golden ratio, about 1.618, which makes partials that never line up into a chord. The 921, kept on AUDIO and on the keyboard, is the modulator, tuned on SEMI a little more than eight semitones up. Its sine passes 902 (2), which the second 911 opens slowly, then an attenuator, into the first 921B’s AC MOD: the amount of FM, the brightness, swells and settles with each note.

sounds.name: Room Resonance Feedback
sounds.ref: In the style of Alvin Lucier — “I Am Sitting in a Room”, 1969
sounds.blurb: A buzzing tone gradually swallowed by a few ringing resonances, as if played again and again in a small room.
sounds.how: Lucier played his voice back into a room until only the room’s resonances were left. Here the 914 is the room: only a few bands are up. Its OUTPUT 1 goes back into the CP3A-M, which also takes the first 921B’s sawtooth, and the mix goes into the 914 again. Each pass through the loop strengthens the bands, so they ring far longer and louder than a filter on its own. The 914’s second OUTPUT is the one we listen to.

sounds.name: Stepped Two-Square Pattern
sounds.ref: In the style of Tonto’s Expanding Head Band — “Zero Time”, 1971
sounds.blurb: Hold one key and the patch plays a stepping pattern of root, fifth and octaves, each step plucked by the filter.
sounds.how: Two square waves at unrelated rates, added in the CP3A-M, give a voltage that steps between four levels. Their gains are set so the steps are musical: the 921 jumps a fifth, the second 921B on LO an octave. That goes into the 921A’s FREQUENCY IN 2, so the first 921B plays the pattern around whatever key is held. The 921’s square is split by a CP35 MULTIPLE into the 961 as well, so each of its edges plucks the 904A through the second 911.

sounds.name: Cross-Patched FM Chaos
sounds.ref: In the style of Morton Subotnick — “Silver Apples of the Moon”, 1967
sounds.blurb: Bubbling, unpredictable electronic tones that tangle into chaos at the start of each note and calm down.
sounds.how: Two 921Bs modulate each other: the second one’s sine goes into the first one’s AC MOD, and the first one’s sine goes back into the second’s, through 902 (2). sounds.name: Northumbrian Smallpipes
sounds.ref: In the style of Kathryn Tickell — Northumbrian smallpipes, “On Kielder Side”, 1984
sounds.blurb: Sweet, staccato pipe chanter over a drone that never stops, playing a lilting jig.
sounds.how: Two 902s make the two halves of the pipes. The second 921B, unlinked, sits on a fixed G whatever key is played: that is the drone, and 902 (2) is simply held open with its FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE. The first 921B, played from the keyboard with a narrow pulse, through the 914 for a reedy chanter, goes through the first 902 with a crisp envelope, because smallpipes are played closed and staccato.

- 902 (2): CONTROL MODE LIN, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 2.

- Cables: 921B (2) SAWTOOTH to 902 (2) SIG IN +; 902 (2) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT R (app).
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.

sounds.name: Elegiac Cello
sounds.ref: In the style of Jacqueline du Pré — Elgar’s Cello Concerto, 1965
sounds.blurb: A dark, bowed cello voice whose vibrato blooms a moment after each note begins, singing a grave melody.
sounds.how: A sawtooth is a bowed string; the 904A softens it, following the keys, and the 914 adds the wooden body’s resonances. A cellist does not start a note with vibrato, so neither does this: the 921’s AUX OUT, the vibrato, passes 902 (2), which the second 911 opens slowly, before it reaches the 921A. The AUX OUT LEVEL is the depth, the 902 is the delay.

sounds.blurb: A twangy, funky clavinet through an envelope wah, quacking on every note of a syncopated riff.
sounds.how: A clavinet is a struck string with two pickups: here a narrow pulse and a sawtooth from the two 921Bs. The 904A, with high REGENERATION and following the keys, is the wah pedal; the second 911 sweeps it on every note through an attenuator, so each note says “wow”.

steps.title: Two pickups
steps.why:
Both 921Bs from the 921A: the first’s RECTANGULAR, narrowed through LINK WIDTH, and the second’s SAWTOOTH mixed into the 904A, which follows the keys; through the 902 with a short, muted decay.
- 921B (1) RANGE 8’.
- 921B (2) RANGE 8’.
- 921A (1) WIDTH 2 · 26 %.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 5, GAIN 2 4, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 904A: FREQUENCY RANGE 2, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 1, REGENERATION 6.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 5 · 140 ms, E SUS 5 · 2.8 V, T3 1.5 · 7 ms.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921A (1) WIDTH TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK WIDTH; 921B (1) RECTANGULAR to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) SAWTOOTH to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 904A SIG IN; CM1A CV 2 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: a nasal, twangy clav.

sounds.name: Upright Walking Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Ron Carter — the Miles Davis Quintet, “E.S.P.”, 1965
sounds.blurb: A woody acoustic bass walking a line in quarter notes, each note a soft thump that blooms and fades.
sounds.how: An upright bass is mostly fundamental with a woody thump at the pluck. A sine and a triangle go through the 904A set low and following the keys; the second 911 opens it for a moment on each note for the finger’s thump, and the first 911 lets the note fade like a gut string.

sounds.name: Erhu Lament
sounds.ref: In the style of the Chinese erhu, after Abing’s “Erquan Yingyue”, 1950
sounds.blurb: A plaintive, nasal bowed fiddle that slides up into each note and sings with a wide, slow vibrato.
sounds.how: The erhu has a small python-skin resonator that gives it a thin, nasal, almost vocal tone; the 914, with its middle bands up and its bottom down, makes it. Erhu players slide into notes: the second 911, inverted by the CP3A-M’s OUTPUT −, pulls the first 921B’s DC MOD a few semitones flat at the start of each note and lets it glide up. The vibrato, from the 921’s AUX OUT, is wide and slow.

steps.title: A nasal bowed string
steps.why:
The keyboard plays the first 921B; its SAWTOOTH into the 914 with the middle up and the bottom down; through the 902.
- 914: LOW PASS 0, 125 Hz 0, 175 Hz 1, 250 Hz 3, 350 Hz 5, 500 Hz 7, 700 Hz 9, 1000 Hz 10, 1400 Hz 8, 2000 Hz 6, 2800 Hz 4, 4000 Hz 2, 5600 Hz 0, HIGH PASS 0.
- 921B (1) RANGE 8’.
- 911 (1): T1 4.5 · 92 ms, T2 6 · 330 ms, E SUS 8 · 4.4 V, T3 5 · 140 ms.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SAWTOOTH to 914 INPUT 1; 914 OUTPUT 1 to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.

sounds.name: Khöömei Overtone Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of Huun-Huur-Tu — Tuvan khöömei throat singing, 1990s
sounds.blurb: A low, growling vocal drone with a whistling overtone melody floating above it, picked out note by note.
sounds.how: A throat singer holds one low note and picks out its harmonics with the mouth. The first 921B is the held voice: unlinked, it never changes pitch. A CP35 MULTIPLE splits it: the 914 shapes one copy into the low vowel; the other goes through the 904A, with high REGENERATION, then the 904B, both tuned by the keyboard. Together they are a narrow band-pass that picks out whichever harmonic of the drone is nearest the key: play the 8th, 9th, 10th and 12th harmonics (G5, A5, B5, D6) and the drone whistles a tune.

steps.title: The held voice
steps.why:
The first 921B, unlinked, at 16’ seven semitones up (a low G); its SAWTOOTH into CP35 MULTIPLE A; one copy into the 914, shaped into a low vowel; the 914 into mixer input 1; the mixer to the output.
- 914: LOW PASS 6, 125 Hz 5, 175 Hz 3, 250 Hz 5, 350 Hz 6, 500 Hz 4, 700 Hz 0, 1000 Hz 0, 1400 Hz 0, 2000 Hz 0, 2800 Hz 0, 4000 Hz 0, 5600 Hz 0, HIGH PASS 0.
- 921B (1): RANGE 16’, FREQUENCY 7 · +7 st.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 4, MASTER GAIN 10.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: 921B (1) SAWTOOTH to CP35 MULTIPLE A (in); CP35 MULTIPLE A 1 to 914 INPUT 1; 914 OUTPUT 1 to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to OUTPUT L (app).
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + from OUTPUT L (app); 911 (1) OUT from 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: a low, growling vowel that never stops.

steps.title: Picking out a harmonic
steps.why:
Another copy into the 904A, ringing, then the 904B; CM1A CV 2 tunes the 904A and CM1A CV 1 the 904B; the 904B into 902 (2), opened by the first 911, into mixer input 2.
- 904A: FREQUENCY RANGE 2, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 8.8.
- 904B: FREQUENCY RANGE LOW, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −0.5.
- 902 (2): CONTROL MODE LIN, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0.
- CP3A-M (1) GAIN 2 10.
- 911 (1): T1 5 · 140 ms, T2 5 · 140 ms, E SUS 10 · 5.5 V, T3 6 · 330 ms.
- Cables: CP35 MULTIPLE A 2 to 904A SIG IN; CM1A CV 2 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1; 904A SIG OUT to 904B SIG IN; CM1A CV 1 to 904B CONTROL INPUT 1; 904B SIG OUT to 902 (2) SIG IN +; 902 (2) SIG OUT + to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (2) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: a high, flute-like whistle singing a melody out of the drone’s own harmonics.
